prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening a new window on the universe

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep the IceCube diffuse flux as my preferred single-part prize. The committee's own tests, as the chair frames them, are independent confirmation, a decisive and traceable contribution, and a clean limit of three names. On the first test the diffuse flux is the strongest of the three leading candidates in the sense I care about: nature gave us a clue that no theory had predicted at that level, and it was seen in several analysis channels (through-going muons, contained cascades, starting events) with different backgrounds and different systematics. That is the discovery, and it does not depend on any one source association. I therefore accept the Chair's sharper wording and would cite only the diffuse flux, leaving TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane out of the citation, so that the claim stays inside what is established. The existential dimension also remains: a particle that crosses the universe unhindered tells us about the most violent accelerators in it. On credit, two names keep the configuration compact and leave room, but I regard the pair as a judgement that the historical record must support, not as an established fact, and I say so openly below.
statement.case_against: Three weaknesses remain and I do not want to hide them. First, attribution: the AMANDA precursor, other IceCube leaders and the analysts who separated the astrophysical flux from atmospheric backgrounds all have claims, and the supplied text does not settle whether Halzen and Karle are the right two. Second, the source picture rests largely on one experiment, which is why the citation must be limited to the diffuse flux; if the committee insists on source confirmation from KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD, the prize is premature. Third, B016 has only two first-place supporters, while B045 appears in seven of eight files; I take seriously that a prize needs a majority in the end, and I would not block B045. My concern there is unchanged: it is a superb instrument and the headline is an accuracy figure, with the redefinition of the second still prospective. B040 has the strongest conceptual argument but, as Mehlig, Olsson and Eriksson themselves say, the three-name cap forces a choice among Mele, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, with Zhang deceased and the 2016 topological prize nearby.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether I would be comfortable with a citation that does not mention TXS 0506+056, and notes that restricting the claim to the diffuse flux also narrows the attribution dispute.
responses.response: Yes, fully comfortable, and I have changed my wording because of your point. My round-1 citation said 'opening neutrino astronomy', which leans on the source results; I now cite only the discovery of the diffuse flux and the new window it opens. I also agree that this narrows the credit question to the concept and construction leadership and the analysis that rejected atmospheric muons and neutrinos. Where I remain less certain than you is whether that narrowing makes Karle's name safe. The committee should ask the external experts for the AMANDA-era record and the discovery-analysis leadership before the vote. If that record points to a different second name I would follow it, so my position is on the discovery and the principle of two names, and only secondarily on the exact pair.

responses.point: Olsson keeps B016 only as an alternative and says she would move toward it if the attribution could be documented more firmly, noting that Karle's role versus the analysts and AMANDA is unclear and that the source identification comes mostly from one experiment.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution worry and I have no better documentation than the supplied text; that is a reason to commission it, not a reason to drop the discovery. On the source identification we are aligned, and the revised citation removes it. I would add that the diffuse flux is the finding the whole collaboration could not have avoided making, because it was found independently in different channels; that lowers the risk that the prize rewards one analysis. Where I differ from you is on B040: you are right that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp keeps the originators and the decisive experiment together, but a prize that explicitly omits the 3D spectroscopy and the HgTe proposal has an attribution problem at least as hard as ours. In IceCube the difficulty is who among many leaders; in B040 the missing names are identifiable and one cannot be recognised.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the optical lattice clock combines a new measurement capability, independent reproduction in several national laboratories, and a clean two-name attribution agreed by all five supporters, and that it is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: Your distinctness argument is a good one, and I accept that the lattice clock addresses Doppler, recoil and quantum-projection-noise limits differently from the ion clock and the comb, so it is not a mere refinement. The independent agreement between laboratories at the 1e-18 level is real scientific evidence, not just popularity. My difference is about what the committee is rewarding: the Nobel Prize goes to discoveries, and the clock's findings about nature (gravitational redshift at millimetre scale, bounds on drifts of constants) are so far bounds and demonstrations, while the redefinition of the second has not happened. I do not think it is wrong to prefer the neutrino flux, but I accept that the credit for B045 is cleaner than for mine and, if the committee cannot document the IceCube credit, I would support B045 over B040 or any quantum-technology candidate.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B040 for its simple general mechanism, a Z2 invariant protecting edge states, with a traceable theory-to-experiment chain, and says recognition is overdue.
responses.response: The conceptual argument is beautiful and I do not dispute it, and I now regard B040 as clearly better than the quantum-technology candidates. But I still cannot rank it first. You say yourself that the cap forces a choice between Mele and Hasan, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp where to look sits outside any permitted trio with Zhang deceased. Whichever trio we choose, one of the strands the committee will be asked about is missing. The 2016 prize also rewarded topological phases and I would need the citation to make clear why this is a new discovery. A two-part 2D/3D split would not help, because it would only increase the number of names beyond the limit and weaken each part. If your group can resolve the credit in a way that I can defend, I would move B040 up.

uncertainties: Whether Halzen and Karle are the two people with the strongest documented claim, given AMANDA-era leaders, other IceCube leaders and the analysis leads for the diffuse-flux discovery.
Whether the committee accepts the diffuse flux alone as the discovery, or insists on independent confirmation of the source associations first, which would make the prize premature.
Whether a prize that three members support first and seven of eight accept as a fallback (B045) should take precedence over a candidate with two first-place votes.
Whether the credit problem in B040 (Hasan, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Zhang's death) can be solved within three names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My connections (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Thomas Van Riet as co-author, the Uppsala string-theory group) do not touch any credited name. I am a theorist outside neutrino astronomy and AMO physics and rely on colleagues and outside experts for experimental credit. I note that I have not changed from my round-1 position, and that Eriksson from Uppsala is a department colleague in a different field, which I do not consider a conflict.
